title: Stove Won't Light at Camp? Buying the Right Camping Gas in Nairobi
meta_title: Camping Gas in Nairobi: 240g or 500g? A Clear Buyer's Guide
meta_description: Camping gas in Nairobi explained: Cadac 500g vs Coleman C300, which stove fits, how much to carry for Mt Kenya, flight rules and where to buy on Thika Road.
excerpt: Buying camping gas in Nairobi starts with your stove's valve. Compare Cadac 500g and Coleman C300 cartridges, plan how much gas to carry and learn how to travel with it safely.

content:
Buying camping gas in Nairobi comes down to one question: what thread or valve does your stove take? Most backpacking stoves use screw-on EN417 cartridges such as the Cadac 500g or the Coleman C300 (240 g of a 70/30 butane-propane mix). Match the valve first, then size your camping gas in Nairobi by how many nights you will cook.

Get the valve wrong and you discover it at Shipton's Camp, at 4,200 m, with a cold dinner ahead. Below we explain the cartridge types sold in Kenya, which one fits which stove, how much gas a weekend or a Mt Kenya trek needs, how to carry it home on a matatu, and where to pick up camping gas in Nairobi on Thika Road.

Quick Facts

  • Most common type: screw-on EN417 cartridges with a 7/16-inch threaded valve, used by most compact hiking stoves.
  • Coleman C300 Performance: 240 g of gas (361 g full), a 70/30 butane-propane blend, 10.5 cm wide.
  • Cadac 500g: butane-propane mix on a standard EN417 thread; Cadac rates it at about 4 hours on a Safari Chef.
  • Cold limit: butane barely vaporises near 0°C, so blends with propane work better on Mt Kenya's frosty camps.
  • Flights: gas cartridges are not allowed in checked or hand luggage, so buy fuel after you land.
  • Where to buy: camping gas in Nairobi is stocked at our shop, Mountain Mall, 3rd Floor, Shop D39, Thika Road.

Which Camping Gas Cartridges Are Sold in Kenya?

Four cartridge styles turn up when you shop for camping gas in Nairobi: screw-on (EN417), pierceable, clip-on or bayonet, and the long aerosol-style cassettes used by tabletop stoves. Each fits only its own kind of stove, so the cartridge on the shelf matters less than the stove already in your cupboard.

The screw-on type is the camping gas in Nairobi that most hikers need. A threaded cartridge screws onto the stove, and a spring valve inside it closes again when you unscrew it, so you can carry a half-used can home and use it next trip. Pierceable cans have no valve at all: the stove punches into the top and has to stay attached until the gas runs out. Clip-on cartridges lock in with a twist and are tied to particular stove makers. Cassettes slot sideways into the flat two-ring or single-ring cookers you see at car-camping sites in Naivasha and around Lake Elementaita.

Cartridge typeHow it connectsCan you remove it part-used?Typical use in Kenya
Screw-on (EN417 thread)7/16-inch thread on topYes, the valve resealsHiking stoves, Mt Kenya and Kilimanjaro treks
PierceableStove punctures the topNo, leave it attachedOlder or budget stoves
Clip-on / bayonetPush and twistYesStoves from the same maker only
Butane cassetteSlides into the side of the cookerYesCar camping, picnics, tabletop cooking

If you are not sure what your stove takes, look underneath the burner. A brass collar with a fine internal thread means screw-on. A spike inside a clamp means pierceable. When in doubt, bring the stove along when you come to buy camping gas in Nairobi and try the fit before you pay.

Cadac 500g or Coleman C300: Which Should You Buy?

The Coleman C300 suits hikers who carry their stove on their back, because it is small and holds 240 g of gas. The Cadac 500g suits group trips and car camping, where twice the fuel in one can matters more than weight. Both use the same EN417 screw thread, and both are popular choices of camping gas in Nairobi.

The Coleman C300 Performance for trekking

The Coleman C300 Performance holds 240 g of a 70/30 butane-propane blend and weighs about 361 g full. It measures 10.5 cm across and 9 cm high, so it nests inside many 1-litre pots with a folded stove beside it. The propane share is the point: propane keeps vaporising far below freezing, while pure butane stalls near 0°C. That makes the C300 the sensible camping gas in Nairobi for anyone heading to Mackinder's Camp, Lake Ellis or the Aberdares moorland. Our older post on the Coleman C300 screw-on gas can covers it in more detail.

The Cadac 500g for groups and car camping

The Cadac 500g cartridge carries 500 g of a butane-propane mix on a standard EN417 thread with a safety valve. According to Cadac's own product page, it screws directly under the Safari Chef HP and runs roughly 4 hours on a Safari Chef, 3 hours on a Citi Chef 40 and 2 hours on a Carri Chef 2. For a family weekend at a campsite near Nanyuki, one Cadac can cover every breakfast and dinner. It is the better-value camping gas in Nairobi per gram, but it is heavier and taller, so it rides better in a car boot than in a 28-litre daypack.

Will a Cadac fit a Coleman stove, or the other way round?

The two best-known brands of camping gas in Nairobi are cross-compatible. A Cadac 500g and a Coleman C300 will each fit any stove made for EN417 screw-on cartridges, whatever brand is printed on the burner. The thread is a shared standard, which you can read about on the EN 417 overview. What changes is the footprint: a tall 500 g can under a small upright burner makes a top-heavy stove, so use a canister stand or a flat rock and keep pots small.

How Much Camping Gas Do You Need for a Hike?

As a rule for camping gas in Nairobi, one 240 g cartridge covers two nights for two people, and two cover a four- or five-day Mt Kenya trek. Plan by burner minutes rather than days, then add a margin for cold mornings and wind.

Here is a worked example using Cadac's own figure of about 4 hours from 500 g on a Safari Chef, which is 240 minutes of burning. If your group cooks two meals a day and each meal takes 20 minutes of flame, that is 40 minutes a day, so one 500 g can lasts about six days in mild weather. Halve the figure for a 240 g can and you get roughly three days. Then cut 25 to 30% from those numbers for high camps, where cold gas burns weaker and you spend longer melting frost off water bottles.

TripGroupGas to carry
Overnight at Mt Longonot base or Hell's Gate campsite2 peopleOne 240 g cartridge (part-used is fine)
Weekend car camping near NaivashaFamily of 4One 500 g cartridge
4-day Mt Kenya trek, self-catering2 peopleTwo 240 g cartridges
5-day Sirimon–Chogoria traverse3 peopleThree 240 g cartridges, or two plus one 500 g left at the car

Weigh any part-used can on a kitchen scale before you go out to buy more camping gas in Nairobi. Subtract the empty weight (about 121 g for a C300, since 361 g full minus 240 g of gas) and you know exactly what is left. That small habit stops the most common mistake we hear about: two half-empty cans in the pack and no full one.

Does Camping Gas Work in the Cold on Mt Kenya?

Camping gas works on Mt Kenya if it contains propane or isobutane and you keep the cartridge warm. Pure butane struggles below about 0°C, and nights at Shipton's and Mackinder's camps regularly drop below freezing, so a blended cartridge and a few simple habits make the difference.

Thin air at altitude actually helps the gas leave the can, because liquids boil at lower temperatures when pressure drops. The problem is temperature, not height. Even good camping gas in Nairobi's shops behaves differently up there: a cartridge that sat outside the tent overnight at 4,200 m may give a weak, flickering flame at 6 a.m. Cadac makes the same point about its own cartridge: butane boils near 0°C, which makes it unsuitable for high altitudes and winter cold, while propane boils at about -42°C.

How to keep a gas cartridge working in freezing weather

  1. Sleep with the cartridge in your sleeping bag's foot box, inside a sock, so it starts the morning near body temperature.
  2. Stand the cartridge on a foam pad or a folded jacket, never directly on frosty rock or snow.
  3. Shield the flame from wind with your body or rocks, but never wrap a windscreen fully around a screw-on cartridge: trapped heat can overheat it.
  4. Carry a lighter as well as the stove's piezo igniter, because igniters often fail when damp or cold.
  5. Buy your camping gas in Nairobi a few days early and start with a fresh can for summit day and use part-used cans at the warmer lower camps.

Can You Carry Camping Gas on a Matatu or a Plane?

You cannot fly with camping gas: cartridges are banned from both checked and hand luggage on commercial flights. On road transport, carry sealed cartridges upright inside your bag, out of the sun, and tell the driver or conductor if asked. Buying camping gas in Nairobi after you land solves the flight problem.

Flying into Nairobi for a climb

Airline dangerous-goods rules treat flammable gas cartridges as forbidden for passengers, and a stove can usually travel in checked baggage only if it is completely empty, clean and free of any fuel smell. Rules vary by airline, so confirm with yours before packing the stove itself. Visitors flying into JKIA for Mt Kenya or Kilimanjaro should plan to pick up camping gas in Nairobi on the way through, together with any other fuel or last items.

Matatus, buses and your own car

Nairobi's matatus and long-distance buses do not publish a clear policy on gas cartridges that we can point you to, so be discreet and sensible rather than assuming it is allowed. When you carry camping gas in Nairobi traffic, keep it sealed, with the stove unscrewed, packed in the middle of your bag. In a private car, store them in the boot rather than on the dashboard or the back shelf, where a Kenyan midday sun can heat a can well past the 50°C that most makers warn against. Never leave cartridges in a closed car parked at a trailhead all day.

What should you check when buying camping gas?

Before paying for any camping gas in Nairobi, check the valve type, the gas blend and the condition of the can. A dented or rusty cartridge should stay on the shelf, whoever is selling camping gas in Nairobi. Use this short checklist:

CheckWhat you want to see
Valve typeMatches your stove (EN417 screw-on for most hiking stoves)
Gas blendButane with propane or isobutane for cold camps; pure butane only for warm lowland trips
Net gas weightPrinted on the can (for example 240 g or 500 g), not just the total weight

Sealed capPlastic cap in place over the valve

Pro Tips for Camp Cooking

  • Test at home: screw the new cartridge onto your stove and light it on the balcony before the trip.
  • Lid on: a pot lid can noticeably cut boiling time and saves gas on every brew.
  • Pre-soak: soak rice, lentils or oats in your water bottle during the afternoon so they cook faster at camp.
  • Simmer low: a medium flame wastes less heat around the sides of a small pot than a full roar.
  • Light first, then pot: keep the headlamp on and the lighter in a chest pocket, as a waterproof rechargeable headlamp frees both hands for the valve.
  • Pack smart: carry the cartridge inside the pot in a 28L day hiking backpack, wrapped in a buff so it does not rattle or scratch.

How Do You Store and Dispose of Gas Cartridges Safely?

Store gas cartridges somewhere cool, dry and shaded, with the cap on, away from cookers and direct sun. Dispose of them only when completely empty, and never leave a can on the mountain. A part-full cartridge is treated as hazardous waste.

Once you get your camping gas in Nairobi home, a shelf in a store room or a cupboard away from the kitchen works well. Avoid the car boot as long-term storage, and avoid the top of a fridge or a sunny window sill. Cadac's guidance for its 500 g can is clear: check the cartridge and the stove connector before each use, and do not use a can showing rust or a connector with corrosion. Damp months between March and May and again from October to December are when rust tends to show, so look at the base of older cans.

What do you do with an empty cartridge?

Run the stove until the flame dies with the valve fully open, then unscrew the can outdoors. Some hikers puncture the empty can with a purpose-made tool before putting it out with scrap metal; never puncture one that still has gas. Carry every empty can back out of the park. Mt Kenya National Park is run by Kenya Wildlife Service, so confirm current park rules and fees on the Kenya Wildlife Service website, and treat every empty can as rubbish you carry home.

Common mistakes with camping gas

Three mistakes with camping gas in Nairobi come up again and again. The first is buying a cartridge type that does not match the stove, often a pierceable can for a screw-on stove. The second is taking only pure butane up to a high camp. The third is cooking inside a closed tent, which risks both fire and carbon monoxide; cook in the porch with the door open, or outside. Avoid those and your stove will be the most reliable thing in your pack. For the wider overnight kit list, our guide to camping gear in Nairobi and the Kenya hiking gear checklist fill in the rest.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use a Coleman gas can on a non-Coleman stove?

A Coleman C300 gas can works on any stove built for EN417 screw-on cartridges, whatever the brand on the burner. The thread is a shared standard, so most compact hiking stoves accept it. It will not fit stoves made for pierceable, clip-on or cassette cartridges. If you are unsure, bring your stove when you buy camping gas in Nairobi and test the fit at the counter first.

How long does a 500g gas canister last when camping?

A 500 g gas canister lasts about 4 hours of burning on a Cadac Safari Chef, according to Cadac, and around 2 to 3 hours on its smaller cookers. For a family cooking two 20-minute meals a day, that is roughly five to six days in mild weather. Cold, wind and high camps can cut that by a quarter or more, so carry a spare.

Is it safe to keep gas cartridges in the car?

Gas cartridges can ride in a car for the drive, but they should not live there. Keep them in the boot, out of direct sun, with the stove unscrewed, and below the 50°C most makers warn about. A car parked in the Kenyan sun heats up fast, so take cartridges with you at the trailhead or keep them in a shaded, ventilated spot.

Why does my gas stove keep going out in the morning?

A gas stove that sputters at dawn usually has a cold cartridge, not an empty one. Butane barely vaporises near 0°C, so pressure drops on frosty mornings at high camps. Warm the can inside your sleeping bag overnight, use a propane or isobutane blend, stand it on a pad rather than frozen ground, and shield the flame from wind.

Can I bring camping gas on a flight to Kilimanjaro?

Camping gas cannot go on a flight to Kilimanjaro or anywhere else, in either checked or hand luggage. Airlines classify flammable gas cartridges as forbidden dangerous goods. Fly with an empty, clean stove if your airline allows it, then buy fuel locally. Many climbers buy their camping gas in Nairobi before driving south through Namanga or Loitokitok.

Final Thoughts

A dented can grabbed in a rush on Friday evening can ruin a camp dinner faster than any bad recipe. Buying camping gas in Nairobi well is mostly about the stove you already own. Check the valve under your stove, choose a butane-propane blend for anything above the forest line, and size your cans by burner minutes instead of guesswork. That covers almost every question about camping gas in Nairobi before a trip.

Your next step before you buy camping gas in Nairobi: count your meals, weigh the half-used can in the cupboard, and pick up what is missing at Mountain Mall or online before Friday's rush.
